data.title: Why infrastructure projects fail at the handover
data.excerpt: The asset is built, the ribbon is cut, and the operating team inherits a system nobody designed for them. Handover has to be designed alongside the system.
data.body:
Infrastructure projects are usually judged at completion. In practice, most of their value or cost is determined after the project team leaves, when the operating team starts making decisions with whatever evidence it inherited.

Handover failures are rarely dramatic. They look like a missing as-built drawing, a spare part with a six-month lead time, or a control sequence nobody can explain.

Design the operating model early

  • Name the future owner before detailed design.

  • Make the as-built requirement part of every package, not a final deliverable.

  • Test the maintenance routine during commissioning, not after.

  • Define the evidence required to accept each system.

Count the cost of ambiguity

A project that saves a month by deferring documentation can cost years of slower maintenance and unsafe improvisation. Handover is when the asset becomes useful, so the paperwork and the training belong to the build.
